items.title: B&Q Limited v Wren Kitchen Limited
items.body:
The Rolls Building
7 Rolls Buildings
Fetter Lane
London EC4A 1NL
Before:
DAVID STONE 
(sitting as a Deputy High Court Judge)
Between:
| B&Q LIMITED | Claimant | 
| - and – |  | 
| WREN KITCHENS LIMITED | Defendant | 
(MS ASHTON CHANTRIELLE instructed by BIRD & BIRD LLP) for the Claimant
(MS JACQUELINE REID AND MR RICHARD ROBERTS instructed by HASELTINE LAKE KEMPNER LLP) for the Defendant
Hearing date: 02 October 2026
APPROVED JUDGMENT
This judgment was handed down remotely at 10.30am on 08 October 2026 by circulation to the parties or their representatives by e-mail and by release to the National Archives.
David Stone (sitting as Deputy High Court Judge):
This is my judgment following the hearing of a disclosure application in this case: there was not sufficient time following the parties’ submissions for an ex tempore judgment to be given.
The Claimant, B&Q Limited (B&Q), has sued Wren Kitchens Limited (Wren) for trade mark infringement under sections 10(1) and 10(3) of the Trade Marks Act 1994 as the result of eight sets of advertisements comparing the prices of B&Q and Wren flat-packed kitchens. By way of examples, those advertisements include statements such as “Wren costs less than B&Q” and “Wren costs 3% - 35% less than B&Q”. These advertisements are said to be contrary to the Business Protection from Misleading Marketing Regulations 2008. Wren denies the claim for trade mark infringement on the basis that the comparisons made were true.
Wren has counterclaimed, also for trade mark infringement, in relation to what is said to be B&Q’s comparative advertising by virtue of B&Q’s reference to comparison tables from a third-party review website (the Kitchen Compare Website) which is operated by Insight Retail Group Limited (IRG), relevantly through a Mr Steve Collinge. The comparisons allegedly referred to are favourable to B&Q. Wren avers that B&Q refers to the Kitchen Compare Website as “independent”, when, Wren says, it is not. Wren has engaged in multiple test purchases at different B&Q stores. For ease I use the expression “test purchases” because that term is generally understood. In fact, Wren has made multiple enquiries at different B&Q stores as if those involved planned to purchase a kitchen, but have never actually done so.
These proceedings were commenced on 2 March 2022. On 30 May 2022, the proceedings were transferred out of the Shorter Trials Scheme. A trial had initially been listed for November 2024. That date was vacated to enable settlement discussions, which did not conclude things. On 8 August 2025 B&Q issued an application to amend its Particulars of Claim to add more claims (taking the total from five to the eight mentioned above). Wren amended its Defence and Counterclaim on 3 July 2023, and again on 16 March 2026. Both sides have already given extended disclosure.
The application that is the subject of this judgment was filed on 3 July 2026 and fell to be determined at the third CCMC in this matter. The first CCMC took place on 19 June 2023 before Master McQuail. The second also took place before Master McQuail, but on 21 August 2023. There were also two disclosure guidance hearings before Master McQuail, on 10 and 16 July 2024. The third CCMC initially came on before me on 14 July 2026. I was able to deal with a number of the issues raised by the parties on that day, but not all of them. A continuation of that CCMC was therefore listed for 5 August 2026 in the first week of the long vacation to try to keep the matter moving by dealing with all issues. Unfortunately, that further hearing day did not conclude the parties’ applications – Wren’s disclosure application remained. I therefore provided the parties with my suggested methodology for resolving the remaining disputes between them, as well as some preliminary indications of my views of the various issues. I adjourned the CCMC in the hope that, over the summer, the parties might be able to resolve what remained in dispute between them without further intervention from the Court. So as to avoid still further delay, I also listed the hearing of the trial for 26 October 2027.
The parties were not able to agree what remained, and so the matter returned to Court for this hearing on the second day of the new court term to determine aspects of Wren’s disclosure application dated 3 July 2026. There is an additional issue of costs budgeting for disclosure – that cannot be determined until after the scope of disclosure is known. The parties have agreed to attempt to resolve costs budgeting between them once this judgment is available to them. If costs budgeting cannot be resolved, I will determine any issues without a hearing.
Ms Ashton Chantrielle appeared for B&Q. Ms Jacqueline Reid and Mr Richard Roberts appeared for Wren and shared the advocacy between them (Mr Roberts addressed me on issue 15B – image searching).
Wren’s Disclosure Application
Wren has applied under paragraph 18 of PD57AD to amend the Disclosure Review Document (DRD) as follows:
To reflect the amended pleadings;
To include “new or extended searches (over different time periods) as a result of B&Q’s failure to disclose documents based on its narrow interpretation of the existing Issue, or as a result of new evidence about when activities occurred”; and
To vary the scope of the search for issue 15 (and to add new issues 15A and 15B) to include image searches for Wren’s device marks.
B&Q has (if I may say so, very sensibly) made a number of offers to try to assuage Wren’s concerns. These include offers to conduct further searches in relation to issues 11A, 12A and 13A (and to an extent 17A) as follows:
B&Q is willing to search the Doncaster and Stockton stores (including the store email addresses and the emails of the store managers) from 1 October 2017 to 31 December 2018 with the search terms that were ordered previously for the original store searches. These two stores have not been searched before, and the timeframe covers the time preceding when Wren alleges there was a ‘big push’ to promote the Kitchen Compare Website;
B&Q is willing to search the documents of the same previously searched 44 head office custodians from 1 October 2017 to 31 December 2017 inclusive across the following search terms:
“Wren” AND “advert”
“Wren” AND “campaign”
“Wren” AND “brand”
“Wren” AND “B&Q”
“Wren” AND “compar*”
“Kitchen Compare”
“Kitchen Compare” AND “Wren”
“KC” AND “Wren”
“IRG” AND “Wren”
B&Q considers that this will uncover any documents showing decision making and instructions relating to use of the Kitchen Compare Website prior to January 2018.
At the hearing on 2 October 2026, Wren embraced these offers, but said they do not go far enough. Wren seeks for the proffered searches to be done with broader search terms and a greater number of custodians. Wren also seeks (independently of the proffered searches) further disclosure in relation to training and promotional material (issues 14A and 17A); B&Q’s involvement with IRG in 2012/2013 (issue 14(b)); the development of the quality criteria assessment (issue 14B) and image searching (issue 15B). It therefore falls to me to determine how much disclosure beyond that offered by B&Q should now be ordered.
The parties each provided various witness statements supporting their positions – none of the deponents was cross-examined. I have had that evidence in mind whilst determining this application.
I should add that the previous disclosure conducted by B&Q was done on the basis that the searches were carried out of the documents of the named custodians and in the listed date ranges on the basis of keywords (as agreed between the parties). The whole cohort of documents was then reviewed as against all disclosure issues. This is also how Wren did its disclosure. An issue which has arisen previously, of B&Q potentially “wearing the wrong goggles” when reviewing a document, was therefore no longer an issue. If a document was caught by a keyword search, it was reviewed for relevance against all issues.
The Law
Paragraph 18 of PD57AD provides:
“18.1 The court may at any stage make an order that varies an order for Extended Disclosure. This includes making an additional order for disclosure of specific documents or narrow classes of documents relating to a particular Issue for Disclosure.
18.2 The party applying for an order under paragraph 18.1 must satisfy the court that varying the original order for Extended Disclosure is necessary for the just disposal of the proceedings and is reasonable and proportionate (as defined in paragraph 6.4).
18.3 An application for an order under paragraph 18.1 must be supported by a witness statement explaining the circumstances in which the original order for Extended Disclosure was made and why it is considered that order should be varied.
18.4 The court’s powers under this paragraph include, but are not limited to, making an order for disclosure in the form of Models A to E and requiring a party to make a witness statement explaining any matter relating to disclosure.
18.5 The court may order a party to request any person to produce for disclosure and inspection any document which may support the case or adversely affect the case of any party to the proceedings.”
Thus, I keep in mind that Wren must satisfy the court that varying the original order for Extended Disclosure (a) is necessary for the just disposal of the proceedings and (b) is reasonable and proportionate.
Wren’s counsel referred me to the judgment of Richard Salter KC (sitting as a Deputy High Court Judge) in Ventra Investments Limited v Bank of Scotland plc [2019] EWHC 2058 (Comm):
“It seems to me that, in such circumstances, what is required from the parties and the Court is a pragmatic, flexible approach to the scope of disclosure, taking into account (as paragraph 9.5 of PD51U requires) ‘all the circumstances of the case, including the factors set out in paragraph 6.4 ... and the overriding objective’. The Court is required to strike a practical balance, in order to decide in each particular case what specific reasonable and proportionate additional disclosure (if any) is necessary for the just disposal of the proceedings. In doing so, the Court is not required to shut its eyes to the practical realities of the litigation.”
I respectfully agree with that statement.
I should add that the parties’ budgets for disclosure come to nearly £1.4 million. That is a very large figure even for a case such as this. I have kept that in mind in my assessment of what is “proportionate” moving forward.
Discussion
I need to say something brief about the background to Wren’s disclosure application. Wren says that most of its current requests for further extended disclosure arise because of the new claims it has made in its Counterclaim. These amendments have mostly come about from additional information discovered by Wren since the proceedings were commenced, including from earlier disclosure completed by B&Q. What Wren has defined as the Store Price Claims are said to arise from B&Q’s use of large upright stands showing information about kitchen retailers’ prices, including Wren. What Wren has defined as the In-store Website Claims are said to arise from B&Q sales staff showing customers the Kitchen Compare Website on computers: it is also alleged that hard copies were posted at workstations used for design appointments. B&Q denies instructing staff to display the price stands, show the Kitchen Compare Website or post hard copies of the comparison tables.
Wren therefore says that disclosure is important because “this is the only way that Wren has to discover B&Q’s activities”. That is not strictly true, as Wren has itself discovered what it says is evidence of B&Q’s activities through test purchases.
As I have already noted, Wren does not consider that B&Q’s offer of further searches goes far enough. Wren seeks:
Wider date ranges;
Broader lists of custodians; and
More keywords to be searched.
B&Q’s position is summarised in the following three paragraphs from the skeleton argument prepared by B&Q’s counsel for this hearing (omitting references):
“10. As explained at the CCMC on 5 August 2026, the ultimate question that the Court needs to consider is whether the newly pleaded allegations in the ADCC actually give rise to a need for further disclosure. It should not be an opportunity for Wren to request that disclosure be carried out again where searches have been done at great time and expense already, simply because they were not satisfied with the outcome and would like to change the goal posts. The Court is reminded the disclosure was already considered at two CCMCs in 2023 and Wren should not be allowed to use this as an opportunity to reopen what was already decided by Master McQuail.
11. Further, the Court is reminded that the Relativity e-disclosure platform team processed in excess of 650GB of B&Q's data in total and stored approximately 300GB within the platform. Of the more than 600,000 documents initially ingested, more than 370,000 were subsequently published for review. 27,541 documents were reviewed and 1,364 items were identified as relevant and ultimately disclosed to Wren. This means that the vast majority of results produced were irrelevant at a cost of over £600,000 so far.
12. The new keywords proposed by Wren are even wider/more generic and do not even include Wren - so it’s hard to see how they are related to the new counterclaims. In any event the requests that continue to be made are disproportionate and amount to fishing.”
Prior to looking specifically at each issue (as I was asked to do), Wren’s counsel made a number of what she described as general points. I summarise these briefly:
Wren alleges that B&Q orchestrated a campaign to “push” the Kitchen Compare Website to its customers from the start of 2018. This is based on evidence of witnesses who say they saw relevant POS material in a small number of B&Q stores (at least two and possibly up to four). B&Q says there was no such campaign or push, but in any event, if there was, Wren says that there ought to be documents relating to it that should have been disclosed. B&Q says that the absence of the disclosure of these documents is because they don’t exist. Wren says it is because B&Q has not searched for the right dates, the right custodians or the right keywords. In addition to the witness evidence relating to the POS materials, Wren relies on an email from IRG telling B&Q that it had won an award, which B&Q then forwarded on 28 November 2017 to various people internally with the words “I am keen to maximise and amplify this support as much as possible … Gemma can you please facilitate”. The reference to Gemma is to Ms Gemma Reilly, a B&Q employee. B&Q has included as custodians several people to whom this email was sent, but not all of them, and not Ms Reilly.
Wren therefore seeks searches from an earlier date, and for a broader range of custodians, including Ms Reilly and the seven other email recipients who have not already been included by B&Q as custodians. B&Q says it has searched the appropriate custodians, because Ms Reilly is junior, and the other custodians will not have documents not caught elsewhere.
On search terms, B&Q has offered further searches on the same search terms as used last time. Wren seeks new and wider search terms. The primary reason given orally was “that obviously did not work last time”. Parenthetically, I add that that statement does not sit comfortably with the basis put for some of the additional extended disclosure requests – to capture documents relating to the newly pleaded issues: rather, it sounds more like a second bite at the cherry.
I turn now to each of the disputed issues, with reference to the DRD. I do not attempt to capture here all the submissions that were put to me, because it is not necessary to do so. In circulating this judgment in draft, I asked the parties to highlight to me any additional areas I should deal with. B&Q’s counsel raised one issue requiring a substantive change, which I deal with in relation to issue 16A below.
11A – In relation to all the Further Price Claims, the Store Price Claims and In-Store Website Claims made by the Claimant, whether the Claimant was acting with due cause
Disclosure has already been provided by B&Q in relation to the issue of due cause in respect of the Email Price Claims, the Further Price Claims and the Quality Claims made by B&Q. Wren now seeks extended disclosure in relation to the new claims added to its Counterclaim.
In relation to the documents in store (as opposed to head office), the date range and the custodians have been agreed. The only thing I need to decide is the keywords. Additionally, Wren seeks the following keywords be searched:
KC;
IRG;
independen* and website;
comparison table; and
Collinge and website.
Wren asserts that this search is reasonable, proportionate and necessary for the just disposal of the proceedings because it directly addresses B&Q’s defence to the extended scope of the counterclaim.
B&Q has provided evidence from the solicitor responsible for the action setting out the searches done in relation to issue 11 and explaining that further searches for these new claims would not uncover anything new given that the existing keyword searches were broad enough in scope that any results relating to the use of the WREN mark would have been caught and disclosed already. B&Q says that the reason it has disclosed no POS materials already is because there are none. All relevant POS materials, B&Q says, have already been searched and disclosed.
I accept B&Q’s position on this issue – or put another way, I am not satisfied that the additional search terms are either (a) necessary for the just disposal of the proceedings or (b) reasonable and proportionate. I accept B&Q’s position, set out in a solicitor’s witness statement over a statement of truth, that these additional search terms would not discover anything further. It is therefore not proportionate to conduct them.
That deals with the store documents – Wren also seeks further extended disclosure from head office custodians. Here, the disagreement was broader, with Wren seeking a search of documents from 1 January 2018 to 30 June 2021, across the same keywords as I have already discussed immediately above, and for a greater number of custodians than the 44 B&Q has already searched. I have dealt with the keyword issue, and it is no different in relation to head office (ie, no additional relevant documents will be discovered).
In relation to the selection of custodians from head office, B&Q has identified 44 whose documents have previously been searched. Wren now says that that is insufficient, and seeks to broaden the cohort, as I have set out above. It asks B&Q to reconsider the list of custodians, but also specifically asks for Ms Reilly to be added, as well as the seven individuals listed in the email of 27 November 2017 to which I have referred above who are not already custodians. In relation to Ms Reilly, whilst I accept that she was at the time a junior employee of B&Q, she was asked to co-ordinate B&Q’s activities on this issue, and it seems to me (just) that there might be documents she holds that have not already come to light through searches of other custodians. Searching one person’s emails will also not overly burden B&Q. I therefore will order that Ms Reilly be added to the list of 44 custodians and that relevant head office searches be conducted of her documents. The position is different with respect to the other seven email recipients. There is no evidence at all that any of them reacted to the email in any way or undertook any steps. Unlike Ms Reilly, they were not individually asked to do so. I therefore reject the request to add them to the list of custodians.
Wren also asks for the proffered search to be extended in date range in relation to head office custodians. As set out by B&Q, it is offered up to 31 December 2017, when the alleged “push” was due to start. Without deciding one way or another whether there was indeed a “push”, it seems to me that if there was, any correspondence could have continued after 31 December 2018. I am therefore persuaded that the search of head office custodians’ emails should be until 31 December 2018, in line with the offered search of the relevant store custodians.
I refuse the application as it relates to issue 11A, other than in relation to adding Ms Reilly as a custodian and extending the search date for head office custodians to 31 December 2018. Wren asked for the issue of custodians to be reassessed in relation to each of the additional requested searches. My ruling in relation to issue 11A applies to all other issues, which means that issues relating to the alleged “push” should include Ms Reilly as an additional head office custodian. I am not ordering any additional custodians in relation to any other issues (such as IRG’s independence from B&Q).
Issues 12A and 13A were said to stand and fall with issue 11A. My ruling above applies mutatis mutandis.
14A – what marketing and public relations services were provided to the Claimant by IRG/the Kitchen Compare Website? What was the extent of the collaboration between the Claimant and IRG/the Kitchen Compare Website in respect of marketing and public relations for the Claimant? What promotional activities did Mr Collinge carry out for the Claimant in the media, in what capacity, and what payments were made by the Claimant to him for such activities?
This issue relates to the independence of IRG and the Kitchen Compare Website from B&Q. Wren considers that the full extent of the relationship between B&Q on the one hand and, on the other hand IRG, the Kitchen Compare Website and Mr Collinge, has not been disclosed. Wren says that very few documents involving Mr Collinge have been disclosed. It seeks searches of:
The 44 head office custodians plus any additional custodians (as discussed above);
In the date range 1 October 2017 to the date of the previous search in 2023; and
Across search terms each of which is a combination of either “Collinge” or “Steve” with a descriptive word such as “marketing”.
Again, B&Q says that these searches have already been carried out in relation to issue 14, and nothing new will be disclosed on the basis of this search. B&Q says that this is an example of Wren being unhappy with the disclosure already provided, and seeking a second bite at the cherry.
I agree with B&Q. I have already dealt with the issue of the 44 custodians. No justification has been provided by Wren for extending the search dates to one month earlier. I also do not consider, based on the evidence before me, that the focus on Mr Collinge is likely to turn up new relevant documents. Wren says that it is possible that B&Q captured relevant documents in its searches, but did not disclose them because of what is said to be a restricted approach to interpretation of issue 14. It does not appear to me that that is what B&Q has done, but, if it were to have, then any such documents would be known adverse documents, and ought to have been disclosed under that heading. The parties have an ongoing obligation to disclose known adverse documents.
I am also concerned that the very broad search terms proposed are likely to generate significant false positives – Steve is a common name, and there are likely to be many emails over a 6-year period which include “Steve” together with “marketing” or the like, but which are irrelevant to these proceedings.
I refuse the application in so far as it relates to issue 14A: this disclosure is not necessary for the just disposal of the proceedings, and it is not reasonable and proportionate.
14B – The involvement of the Claimant (if any) in the creation of the Kitchen Compare website’s quality assessment criteria or process
B&Q’s position is that the Kitchen Compare Website is independent. Wren says it has uncovered evidence that the Kitchen Compare Website was created at B&Q’s request. Wren therefore seeks searches:
In the date range 1 January 2012 to 30 April 2013 when the Kitchen Compare Website was first set up;
For an as yet unidentified number of custodians;
For the search terms:
Collinge
Kitchen Compare
IRG.
B&Q says that it has already provided disclosure on this issue under issue 14(c) “the involvement of the Claimant (if any) in the compilation and/or assessment of lowest price and quality reviews or awards on the Kitchen Compare Website”. That is a broad issue, and, in my judgment, captures the issue on which Wren seeks further extended disclosure. I do not consider that the ASA document relied on by Wren alters that position. The date range is a different issue, given that B&Q has not searched as early as 2012/2013. In my judgment, that does not matter. B&Q denies having been involved in the establishment of the Kitchen Compare Website, and there is before me no solid evidence to the contrary. In any event, Wren alleges that the “big push” at B&Q to refer to the Kitchen Compare Website did not start until 2018 – which suggests that it was, at best, a very long-term play were it to be true that B&Q encouraged the set-up of the Kitchen Compare Website in 2012, but then did not seek to take advantage of it until 2018. That would be commercially very unusual indeed. Finally, the pleaded issues before the court relate to the state of play in (at the earliest) late 2017 and following – such that even if B&Q had been involved in the Kitchen Compare Website in 2012, the position could well have changed by 2017, and it is the position in 2017 that matters. The requested searches are not necessary or proportionate.
I therefore refuse extended disclosure on the basis of issue 14B. I am not satisfied that this disclosure is necessary for the just disposal of the proceedings or is reasonable and proportionate.
14(b) - the relationship between the Claimant and IRG including: involvement if any of the Claimant in the formation and operation of the [Kitchen Compare W]ebsite
Additional extended disclosure under issue 14(b) is put by Wren on a different basis. Disclosure has already been completed in relation to issue 14(b), which covers the relationship between IRG and B&Q. Wren now seeks a wider date range for the search. At the second CCMC heard in August 2023, the scope of the date range for the search was discussed. Wren now says that, having looked at the documents already disclosed by B&Q, it is apparent that the searches failed to capture B&Q’s involvement (if any) in the formation of the Kitchen Compare Website, which was set up in 2012. Wren therefore seeks to extend the period of the search already undertaken to cover the period 1 January 2012 to 30 April 2013. For the reasons already set out above in relation to issue 14B, I also refuse the application in so far as it relates to issue 14(b): this disclosure is not necessary for the just disposal of the proceedings and it is not reasonable and proportionate.
15B: image searching in relation to issue 15 - The extent of the Email Price Claims, Further Price Claims and Quality Claims made by the Claimant (the Defendant having set out examples of such claims in its pleaded case) in emails or other correspondence between its employees to potential customers.
Issue 15 has already been searched by B&Q using text-based searching on the basis of the order made by Master McQuail. That search was limited to a text search of documents from 30 stores over two six-week periods. Wren now seeks an image search across the 30 stores for a four-week period in March 2021. The Master did not preclude Wren from asking for image-based searching in due course – but she declined to order it including because of the then estimated cost of the searching (£400,000). The parties are now agreed that the costs are likely to be closer to £100,000, including because of the improvement in technology since 2023. Wren has identified a proprietary AI tool, launched in January 2025, capable of analysing content and identifying relevant images.
Wren also says that the importance of this search has increased. This is because B&Q has pleaded that the use of Wren’s marks was “negligible and/or insignificant” and therefore de minimis. Wren therefore seeks image searches in order to disclose the full extent of uses of Wren’s marks in communications from B&Q.
Further, Wren says that documents already disclosed also show Wren’s marks in an image, such that Wren says there are likely to be other such documents available to be disclosed if an image search is conducted.
B&Q says that it has already undertaken text searches, and a form of image search. Further, B&Q says that the original searches under issue 15 were set for date ranges in early 2022 and early 2023 to reflect the periods in which Wren conducted its test purchases of B&Q kitchens. B&Q says that the March 2021 dates now proposed by Wren pre-date the pleaded issues by some 12 months. B&Q also says that this issue has been created in essence by Wren’s test purchases (which Wren has declined to detail) – highlighting that it is actually Wren’s test purchases which have generated the disclosed “hits” rather than (potentially in all but one case) actual customers.
I agree with B&Q’s submissions. As set out above, the costs of disclosure in this case are already high – increasing them by a further £100,000 would, in my judgment, be disproportionate, given what appears to be the unlikelihood of identifying anything relevant in the further searches. Whilst the additional £100,000 is less than the £400,000 rejected by the Master, it is still a large sum of money, even in the context of this hard-fought litigation. I am not satisfied that the image searching is necessary for the just disposal of the proceedings, but even if I were, I would consider it not to be reasonable or proportionate.
16A – Information available to the Claimant and/or available to consumers verifying the Store Price Claims and/or the In-store Website Claims
A search has already been carried out under issue 16 for the other claims pleaded – issue 16A reflects the additional claims added as part of Wren’s amendments to its Counterclaim.
Given the amendment to the Counterclaim, and that this issue has not previously been searched, I will allow the application in so far as it relates to issue 16A.
Having reviewed a draft of this judgment, B&Q’s counsel submitted that it was not clear to B&Q what the parameters for this search (dates, custodians, keywords) should be as, she said, this was not raised in Wren’s application, correspondence or submissions. Further, she submitted that the search that had been carried out for issue 16 was in relation to 8 store email addresses and each store had specific dates to search across three keywords: “Wren” AND “price”; “Wren” AND “quality”; and “Wren” AND “cost”. She submitted that if that same search is done again, the same documents would turn up.
Wren’s counsel responded that the parties should be able to agree search terms and dates. It seems to me that it would be best for them to try to do so, and, if not, I can make a decision without a hearing.
17A – (a) Whether and what instructions and/or training were given by the Claimant’s managers and/or directors and/or IRG’s staff or directors to B&Q showroom managers and staff in relation to: (i) making the Email Price Claims, Further Price Claims and Quality Claims in the pleaded advertising emails, the Store Price Claims and/or In-store Website Claims; and (ii) refer to (1) the Kitchen Compare website, including any use made of the Kitchen Compare Website when marketing and selling kitchens in the Claimant’s stores; and/or (2) Wren; (b) How did the Store Price Claims and In-store Website Claims come to be made by the Claimant’s sales staff? This includes how POS material was designed, approved, produced, paid for and distributed.
Wren seeks documents showing what training was carried out in respect of the “push” to promote the Kitchen Compare Website. It therefore seeks searches:
From 1 October 2017 to 30 June 2021 (emails) and to 1 January 2018 (documents);
In relation to the 44 head office custodians as reconsidered (for which, see above); and
Across an array of search terms.
Wren says that documents already disclosed show that Mr Collinge’s involvement has been greater than portrayed by B&Q – it is said that he has provided training to B&Q staff. The earlier date range is sought because of evidence that B&Q gave its instructions for the new year from on or about 1 October in the previous year.
B&Q says that any training materials have already been disclosed. Whilst these issues are new, the previously done searches cover them, and searches were conducted from 1 November 2017 (Wren seeks a month earlier – 1 October 2017). B&Q has also provided evidence that the head office team did not provide any central instructions to its showroom staff relating to use of the Kitchen Compare Website.
In my judgment, based on the evidence before me, the additional searches requested by Wren are unlikely to turn up any relevant documents, given the broad searches that have already been undertaken. It does not seem likely to me that a document would exist from October 2017 directed at trading from January 2018 that was not caught by a search of documents from 1 November 2017. In my judgment, the additional searches offered by B&Q deal with any lacunae in the earlier searches. I am therefore not satisfied that this additional search is necessary for the just disposal of the proceedings or is reasonable and proportionate.
Result
Wren’s disclosure application succeeds only in relation to issues 11A, 12A and 13A (one additional custodian and a longer date range in relation to head office custodians) and 16A. B&Q should now conduct the additional disclosure searches it has offered, as modified by this judgment.

items.title: Sheet metal fabrication company fined £48,000 after employee suffers life-changing injury
items.summary: Employee lost part of his right thumb and suffered a crush injury to his hand during a manual handling task, just days after a near-identical incident HSE investigation found employee had not been given clear instructions on how to carry out task safely Worker was amateur boxer before hand injury – describing hobby as his […]
items.body:
- Employee lost part of his right thumb and suffered a crush injury to his hand during a manual handling task, just days after a near-identical incident
- HSE investigation found employee had not been given clear instructions on how to carry out task safely
- Worker was amateur boxer before hand injury – describing hobby as his ‘whole life’
- A had occurred in the days before this one.
Fitzpatrick Fabrications Ltd, a sheet metal fabrication company in Lancashire, has been fined £48,000 after an employee lost part of his right thumb and suffered a crush injury to his hand during a manual handling task.
On 24 October 2024, at around 11.30am, Mr Todd Marshall, a welder/fabricator, was working at the Fitzpatrick Fabrications factory at Malvern Mill, Nelson. The job involved welding and fabricating large pieces of stainless steel to form a finished hopper.
The hopper consisted of five component parts, which needed to be welded together. When each side of the hopper was welded, it needed to be lifted and repositioned so the next side could be welded.
Mr Marshall was carrying out this task on his own, holding the larger side of the 133kg hopper in the air while the smaller side rested on a desk. The hopper slipped on the smooth desk and came down onto his hand, causing a crush injury and partial loss of his right thumb.
An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that the company had not conducted a risk assessment for the task and no safe system of work was in place. As a result, workers had not been given clear instructions on how to perform the task safely.
Upon further investigation, HSE found that a near-identical incident had occurred in the days leading up to this one.
HSE guidance states that employers must assess the risks associated with manual handling and take appropriate steps to avoid hazardous manual handling operations where reasonably practicable, or reduce the risk of injury where they cannot be avoided. The Manual Handling Assessment Charts (MAC Tool) can also help employers assess the most common risk factors associated with lifting and carrying activities.
In a statement, Mr Marshall said:
“Things I used to do without thinking are now hard for me. I need two hands to do something as simple as pick up small things. I struggle fastening buttons or zips. I was an amateur boxer before my injury. Boxing was my whole life. It wasn’t just a pastime or hobby. I think I could have gone further with it, but now I’ll never know.”
Fitzpatrick Fabrications Ltd, of Malvern Mill, Waterford Street, Nelson, pleaded guilty to breaching Regulation 4(1) of the Manual Handling Operations Regulations 1992. The company was fined £48,000 and ordered to pay £10,089 in costs at Warrington Magistrates’ Court on 6 October 2026.
HSE Inspector Derek McLauchlan said:
“This was a wholly preventable incident which has had a profound and long-lasting impact on Todd Marshall’s life, made more shocking by the fact a near-identical incident had taken place just days before.
“Businesses should always give thought to the safest way to undertake manual handling operations; this means carrying out a robust assessment of the risks, and considering tools such as the Manual Handling Assessment Chart (MAC Tool) to help plan the task.
“The company failed in its duty to properly plan this task, and the fine imposed should serve as a clear reminder to everyone that HSE will hold to account those who fail to keep their workers safe.”
This HSE prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer Tom Ledden-Rocks and paralegal officer Stephen Grabe.

items.title: Leading firearms firm handed six figure fine after worker suffers burns
items.summary: Woman suffered burns to hands, face and legs when disposing of pyrotechnic waste at site in Lincolnshire GMK Limited had not risk assessed the work or provided her with suitable PPE HSE investigation also found company was in breach of its explosive licence One of the country’s leading distributors of firearms for sports shooting and […]
items.body:
- Woman suffered burns to hands, face and legs when disposing of pyrotechnic waste at site in Lincolnshire
- GMK Limited had not risk assessed the work or provided her with suitable PPE
- HSE investigation also found company was in breach of its explosive licence
One of the country’s leading distributors of firearms for sports shooting and law enforcement has been fined £800,000 after a worker suffered burns at its site in Lincolnshire.
The 36-year-old was disposing of waste pyrotechnic material inside a manufacturing facility when it ignited and caused burns to her hands face and legs. An investigation by Britain’s workplace regulator found there was no suitable risk assessment and no safe system of work carried out by GMK Limited when the incident happened at the company’s Faldingworth base on 10 January 2023.
The woman had been working alongside a colleague disposing of waste pyrotechnic composition inside the production building at the site. The pair had been using a metal tray designated for the destruction of excess powders. However, during the process, a quantity of pyrotechnic composition came into contact with the hot tray and ignited unexpectedly, resulting in a flash that caused burns.
An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) established that GMK Limited permitted the woman to carry out a disposal method for waste pyrotechnic composition that had no safe system of work. They had also failed to carry out a risk assessment and the activity was undertaken in an unlicensed part of the building.
The investigation also identified that the company failed to provide the woman with suitable personal protective equipment (PPE), which, if provided and correctly used, may have prevented or significantly reduced the injuries she sustained.
Although GMK Limited had an established and recognised method for the disposal of waste pyrotechnic substances and articles, this approved procedure was not followed on the day of the incident. Instead, the unapproved disposal method carried out within the production building had been informally used for a number of years and had been undertaken on multiple occasions without proper assessment, controls, or oversight.
The industry guidance for the Safe Management of the Disposal of Explosives details what the explosives industry expects at a burning / disposal ground and how it is managed. It was a reasonably practicable to ensure that disposal took place at the designated area using the prescribed methods in the guidance document.
During the investigation HSE also identified that GMK Limited were in breach of their explosives licence in that they were storing pyrotechnics in areas within the production building that were not licensed for that purpose.
GMK Limited, of Fareham, Hampshire, pleaded guilty to breaching Section 2(1) of the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 and Regulation 7 of the Explosives Regulations 2014. The company was fined £800,000 and ordered to pay £10,306 in costs at Birmingham Magistrates’ Court on 2 October 2026.
After the hearing, HSE inspector Philip Smith said:
“For a leading company such as GMK to fail in the most basic of ways is hugely concerning.
“This young woman’s injuries could have easily been avoided with the implementation of safe working practices and use of the correct PPE.
“I hope the scale of fine handed out sends a message to industry that failing to protect workers will result in HSE taking action.”
The prosecution was brought by HSE advocate Tom Ledden-Rocks, enforcement layers lawyers Laura Lax and James Towey and paralegal officer Sarah Thomas.

items.summary: 59-year-old father of two was killed when he fell from first floor The work had not been properly planned or measures put in place Falls from height remain leading cause of fatalities in construction industry An Oxfordshire-based construction company has been fined £120,000 after a carpenter died when he fell through an unsafe first floor […]
items.body:
- 59-year-old father of two was killed when he fell from first floor
- The work had not been properly planned or measures put in place
- Falls from height remain leading cause of fatalities in construction industry
An Oxfordshire-based construction company has been fined £120,000 after a carpenter died when he fell through an unsafe first floor while carrying out refurbishment work.
W G Carter Limited, of Appleton, was sentenced following the death of 59-year-old Richard “Felix” Roper, who fell from height while working at a domestic property in Gloucestershire.
Mr Roper, a father of two, had been carrying out work on the first floor of Manor Barn House, Nether Westcote, on 30 August 2022, where extensive repairs were being undertaken to replace rotten floor joists and floorboards.
He had been tasked with replacing damaged floor joists while other workers removed sections of flooring in the same area. Large parts of the first-floor structure had been stripped back, leaving open gaps between joists. In addition, some joists were either missing altogether or had not been secured.
It was while working in these conditions, Mr Roper fell from the first floor to the concrete ground floor below. He sustained severe head injuries and died in hospital the following day.
A joint investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) and Gloucestershire Police found that the work at height had not been properly planned, appropriately supervised, or carried out safely.
The investigation identified several serious failings. Workers, including Mr Roper, were able to access areas of the first floor where flooring and structural supports had been removed, despite there being insufficient measures in place to prevent falls. At the same time, other workers were continuing to remove floorboards, creating and increasing the risk of falling from height.
Following the incident, HSE served a Prohibition Notice, stopping further work at height until adequate safety measures had been introduced.
Falls from height remain the leading cause of workplace death and injury with the latest statistics from HSE showing that they account for over a quarter of all work related deaths in 2025/26.
HSE guidance states what an employer must do to protect their employees from falls from height including making sure work is properly planned, supervised and carried out by competent people.
The investigation found that W G Carter Limited had failed to adequately plan the work and implement suitable measures to prevent workers from falling. After the incident, the company adopted a safer method of working, installing floor joists from below using appropriate work-at-height equipment and preventing access to the first floor while the work was being undertaken.
On 24 September 2026, at Bristol Magistrates Court, W G Carter Limited, of 81A Eaton Road, Appleton, Oxfordshire, pleaded guilty to breaching Regulation 4(1) of the Work at Height Regulations 2005. The company was fined £120,000 and ordered to pay costs of £5,247.
HSE principal inspector James Lucas said:
“Due to the failings of this company, a man lost his life.
“Every year, workers are killed or suffer life-changing injuries because work at height has not been properly planned or suitable safeguards have not been put in place.
“Had appropriate controls been in place, Felix’s death could have been prevented.”
“Our thoughts remain with Felix’s family. He was a valued colleague and a much-loved father of two who lost his life in circumstances that should never have arisen.”
The prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer Gemma Zakrzewski, enforcement advocate Rowena Goodwin and paralegal officer Hannah Snelling.
Further information:
- The Health and Safety Executive (HSE) is Britain’s national regulator for workplace health and safety. We are dedicated to protecting people and places, and helping everyone lead safer and healthier lives.
- More information about the legislation referred to in this case is available.
- Further details on the latest HSE news releases is available.
- HSE does not pass sentences, set guidelines or collect any fines imposed. Relevant sentencing guidelines must be followed unless the court is satisfied that it would be contrary to the interests of justice to do so. The sentencing guidelines for health and safety offences can be found here.

items.title: Aggregates company fined after worker killed in conveyor crush
items.summary: Worker died from crush injuries after being drawn into machinery through a gap in fixed guarding. Company fined and ordered to pay contribution to costs after pleading guilty to breaching PUWER 1998. Gill Aggregates Limited, which operates a site in Dagenham, East London, has been fined £24,000 after one of its workers was drawn into […]
items.body:
- Worker died from crush injuries after being drawn into machinery through a gap in fixed guarding.
- Company fined and ordered to pay contribution to costs after pleading guilty to breaching PUWER 1998.
Gill Aggregates Limited, which operates a site in Dagenham, East London, has been fined £24,000 after one of its workers was drawn into machinery and suffered fatal crush injuries.
Manjit Kumar, 34, was working as a production operative for Gill Aggregates Limited at its East London Aggregate Depot in Halyard Street, Dagenham, on 24 June 2020, when the incident occurred. He was operating a bag flattening conveyor system forming part of a larger piece of machinery.
Mr Kumar was drawn into the compression conveyor through an opening in the guarding. His colleagues raised the alarm and stopped the machine, and the guarding had to be dismantled so that he could be retrieved. The crush injuries were so significant that he died in hospital a few days later.
An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that the company, which provides pre-packed and loose aggregates and haulage services to builders’ merchants and the construction industry, had failed to prevent access to dangerous parts of the machinery. Although a fixed guard was fitted around the compression conveyors, it contained an opening measuring approximately 600mm wide by 335mm high, which allowed access to the dangerous moving parts. Following the incident, further guarding was installed to prevent access to the compression conveyors.
The law requires that employers must take effective measures to prevent access to dangerous parts of machinery, or stop their movement before any part of a person enters a danger zone. The measures include fixed enclosing guards and, where these are not practicable, other guards or protection devices. Hazards from machinery should be identified as part of the risk assessment, which should identify measures to reduce the risks those hazards present.
Gill Aggregates Ltd, of Botany Marsh, Lower Road, Northfleet, Kent, pleaded guilty to breaching Regulation 11(1) of the Provision and Use of Work Equipment Regulations 1998. The company was fined £24,000 and ordered to pay a contribution towards costs of £43,000 at Snaresbrook Crown Court on 28 September 2026.
HSE Inspector Adepeju Sogadgi said:
“This was a tragic incident that resulted in Manjit losing his life.
“The risks associated with dangerous moving machinery are well known. Employers must ensure that effective measures are in place to prevent workers from gaining access to dangerous parts.
This HSE prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement lawyer Edward Parton, supported by paralegal Anushka Lulith.

items.title: Transport for London convicted after “vibrant member of community” Grace Mecaley, 74, killed while crossing road
items.summary: 74-year-old Grace Mecaley killed after being struck by a bus while using a pedestrian crossing TfL failed to properly manage risks to pedestrians at Walthamstow Bus Station Similar collision in 2022 and five near misses recorded in the two days before Grace’s death Transport for London (TfL) has been convicted and fined £2 million after […]
items.body:
- 74-year-old Grace Mecaley killed after being struck by a bus while using a pedestrian crossing
- TfL failed to properly manage risks to pedestrians at Walthamstow Bus Station
- Similar collision in 2022 and five near misses recorded in the two days before Grace’s death
Transport for London (TfL) has been convicted and fined £2 million after a 74-year-old woman was struck by a bus and killed while using a pedestrian crossing at Walthamstow Bus Station.
Mrs Grace Mecaley was walking home after shopping on Walthamstow High Street on 15 December 2023 when she was struck by a double-decker bus.
At around 5pm, Mrs Mecaley was crossing the road from Rose Bank Villas at an authorised pedestrian crossing. She was around two-thirds of the way across when a number 212 bus rounded the corner and struck her.
Mrs Mecaley suffered fatal injuries and was pronounced dead at the scene.
An investigation by the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) found that TfL had failed to ensure pedestrians and vehicles could circulate safely at the bus station.
The crossing was positioned at the apex of a bend, where buses turned into the station. Its position and the angle at which buses approached meant drivers could turn towards the crossing without a clear view of its full length.
The ‘red carpet’ crossing was intended to give pedestrians priority. However, the layout created ambiguity over right of way and increased the risk of a collision.
TfL’s failure to manage the risks at the crossing persisted for years. Despite a pedestrian being struck by a bus in similar circumstances in April 2022, TfL failed to risk assess the crossing. CCTV footage also captured five near misses in the two days before Mrs Mecaley was killed.
HSE’s investigation also found TfL had failed to adequately monitor bus drivers operating at the station.
The Approved Code of Practice (ACOP) for the Workplace (Health, Safety and Welfare) Regulations 1992 provides guidance on keeping pedestrians and vehicles safe, including clearly marking traffic routes and avoiding sharp or blind bends where possible.
Transport for London (TfL) of 5 Endeavour Square, London, E20 1JN, pleaded guilty to a charge of breaching Regulation 17(1) of the Workplace Health, Safety, and Welfare Regulations 1992.
TfL was fined £2 million and ordered to pay £5081 in costs at Westminster Magistrates’ Court on 25 September 2026.
Speaking at Westminster Magistrates’ Court HSE Inspector Laurence Goodacre said:
“Our deepest sympathies remain with Grace’s family who are represented here today by her son. Grace was a vibrant member of her community and her loss will be deeply felt.
“Grace was simply walking home after shopping when she was struck and killed while using an authorised pedestrian crossing.
“TfL had a responsibility to keep pedestrians safe, but its failings meant Grace never made it home.
“Grace died just days before Christmas and her family will continue to feel that loss particularly deeply at what should be a happy time of year.
“I hope today’s sentence provides them with some measure of comfort, knowing that those responsible for her death have been held to account.”
This HSE prosecution was brought by HSE enforcement Lawyers Rebecca Schwartz and Jon Mack and paralegal officer Thomas Smith.
